title: Snow White Builds an Awareness Program
context_md:
Snow White has just been promoted to **GRC Analyst** at *Seven Dwarfs Mining*, a 400-person mining and refining company headquartered in the Black Forest. Last quarter, Grumpy clicked a link in an email claiming to be from the Queen's Royal Bank, exposing payroll data for the entire mining crew. The CEO, Doc, has asked Snow White to stand up a formal security awareness program before the next audit.

A junior analyst has handed Snow White a draft document mixing several governance tiers together in one file. Before Snow White can finalize the program, she has to split this draft into the correct document types — and pick the right metrics, framework, and ownership tool for the program itself.

The audit committee has signaled they care most about IT process maturity rather than ITSM service delivery.
artifact_md:
1. *Seven Dwarfs Mining is committed to protecting employee and customer information from unauthorized disclosure or loss. Senior management endorses this commitment.*
2. *All employees must complete security-awareness training within 30 days of hire and annually thereafter. All employee passwords must be a minimum of 14 characters and rotated every 90 days.*
3. *Recommended: Use a passphrase of four or more random words rather than a complex random string — it is easier to recall and mathematically harder to crack.*
4. *Help Desk — Resetting a locked account:* (a) verify employee identity via callback to the number stored in HR; (b) in Active Directory, right-click the user → Reset Password; (c) force password change at next logon; (d) log the reset in the ITSM ticket.
prompt_md: Help Snow White classify each line of the draft and finish her program plan by selecting the correct option for each blank. Click **Check answers** when you are done.
body_md:
Looking at the draft excerpt above:

Line 1 — the board-endorsed intent statement — belongs in a **{{intent_doc}}**. Line 2 — the mandatory, measurable requirements about training cadence and password length — belongs in a **{{mandatory_doc}}**. Line 3 — the *recommended* passphrase tip — belongs in a **{{optional_doc}}**. Line 4 — the help desk's exact click-by-click reset steps — belongs in a **{{stepwise_doc}}**.

With the documentation split correctly, Snow White moves on to the program itself. To measure whether awareness is improving, she will track the **{{primary_metric}}** on monthly simulated phishing campaigns. Because the audit committee cares about IT governance maturity, she will align her control objectives to **{{framework}}** rather than the alternative service-management framework. Finally, to make sure responsibility for incident response is unambiguous across Doc, Grumpy, and Snow White herself, she will document roles using a **{{responsibility_tool}}**.

intent_doc.explanation: Line 1 is a high-level, board-endorsed statement of intent — no specific metrics, no steps. That is the defining shape of a Policy.

mandatory_doc.explanation: Line 2 is mandatory *and* measurable (30 days, 14 characters, 90 days) — the hallmark of a Standard. A Policy would say 'employees must be trained' without naming the numbers.

optional_doc.explanation: Line 3 opens with 'Recommended' — the word that signals a Guideline. Employees may use a different method as long as the Standard's 14-character minimum is still met.

stepwise_doc.explanation: Line 4 is an ordered, click-by-click set of instructions tied to a specific tool (Active Directory). Procedures live closest to the technology and are rewritten whenever the tool changes.

primary_metric.explanation: Click-through rate on simulated phishing is the standard KPI for awareness programs — it directly measures the behavior the program is trying to change.

framework.explanation: COBIT focuses on IT governance and process maturity, which is what the audit committee asked for. ITIL is the service-management alternative.

responsibility_tool.explanation: A RACI matrix assigns Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed roles — the canonical tool for clarifying who-does-what in incident response.
